result:
Solution 1 is correct, and Solutions 2 and 3 are not.

The key constraint is that $P$ has integer coefficients, not just integer values. Writing $P(x)=\sum_j b_j (x)_j$ with $b_j\in\mathbb{Z}$ (the falling factorial basis is a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$), the condition $p^k \mid P(m)$ for all $m$ becomes $v_p(b_j)+v_p(j!)\ge k$ for all $j$. The coefficient condition is $\sum_j b_j s(j,n)=1$. This is solvable exactly when some $j\ge n$ has $v_p(j!)\ge k$ and $p\nmid s(j,n)$, so
$$k(n,p)=\max\{v_p(j!) : j\ge n,\ p\nmid s(j,n)\}.$$

Modulo $p$, the rising factorial $y(y+1)\cdots(y+j-1)$ factors as $(y^p-y)^m\,g_r(y)$ with $j=pm+r$, where $g_r$ has lowest term of degree at most 1. For $j=pn$, the $y^n$ coefficient is $(-1)^n\not\equiv 0$. For $j>pn$, the lowest-degree term of the product exceeds $n$, so $p\mid s(j,n)$. Hence the maximum is at $j=pn$:
$$k(n,p)=v_p((pn)!)=n+v_p(n!).$$

Summing: $\sum_{n=11}^{15} n = 65$ for each prime, giving $130$. The extra valuations are $v_{11}$ contributing $5$ and $v_{13}$ contributing $3$ (from $n=13,14,15$). Total $138$.

Solution 1 gets $138$. Solution 2 uses only the top coefficient and ignores the higher-degree terms, giving $k=v_p(n!)$ and the wrong total $8$. Solution 3 relies on an unverified formula, $\sum_i\lfloor n/(p^i(p-1))\rfloor$, which gives $9$ and contradicts $k(n,p)=n+v_p(n!)$ (e.g., $k(11,11)=12$, not $1$).

VERDICT 1: ACCEPT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
